meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Strong contractions.
My butterfly.
Come on, everything is fine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where is the menu for breakfast?
And where is my pizza?
Where are our beautiful rose petals?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'your, yours (polite or plural)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This does not interrupt your rest.
And where is your top management?
Who are your rivals?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('the main thing').

examples.trans: And where is your top management?
The main thing is, don't worry.
This is the main street.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'чальство'). Common neuter noun meaning 'management / bosses' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: And where is your top management?
The management signed an important order.

examples.text: Успокойся, начальство просто не знает всей правды.
examples.trans: Calm down, the leadership simply does not know the whole truth.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'we await', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: Don't wait for me.
I'm waiting for you.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'she; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Она нашла нас на новом месте.
examples.trans: She found us at the new place.
That is it, she got really offended.
She is not answering her phone.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, after', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: They came yesterday and placed an order.
Were they here yesterday?

examples.text: Сегодня вечером я сделаю ей предложение!
examples.trans: Tonight I will propose to her!

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'couple' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Ей нравится, когда ей доверяет парень.
examples.trans: She likes it when her boyfriend trusts her.

examples.text: Он ведёт себя как ревнивый парень.
examples.trans: He behaves like a jealous boyfriend.
I am her boyfriend, got it?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'hours' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I must not get nervous right now at all.
And right now excuse me.
Listen, tell me right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'this, it (is)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What kind of nonsense is this?
This is a service for our guests.
This does not interrupt your rest.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You two argue really coolly.
Why is there a meat shortage here?
In short, he knows what it is for.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('tasty').

examples.trans: Well, is it a tasty banana?
This is a very delicious pizza.
At home they cook badly.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'pizza' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я хочу, чтобы ты приготовил пиццу.
examples.trans: I want you to make a pizza.
What kind of pizza could there be here?
I said pizza, so pizza it is.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: The hotel manager goes straight to the room.
Let go of him right now!

examples.text: Куда мы спрячем эту большую коробку?
examples.trans: Where will we hide this big box?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Он ведёт себя как ревнивый парень.
examples.trans: He behaves like a jealous boyfriend.

examples.text: Я как будто в театр сходил.
examples.trans: It is as if I went to the theater.
And how should I react?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I am with you.
My butterfly.
Take more air in.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'like', paired with 'полюбить'.

examples.trans: You love Katya, after all.
I love our town very much.
Do you like gum?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: How do you know? Does it show already?
It is clear that professionals made it.
You can see at once she's a businesswoman.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what, that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What is with you, mommy, huh?
Did something happen?
What kind of nonsense is this?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'did, were doing', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: Please make coffee for the tables.
What are you doing in there right now?
That is it, she got really offended.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'фессионал'). Common masculine noun meaning 'professionals' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It is clear that professionals made it.
He's a real professional.
There's nothing but professionals here.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мне нужно доверие, а не ревность.
examples.trans: I need trust, not jealousy.
With them, if you are jealous, it is bad.
Yeah? Come on then, let's go.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We are almost there already.
We work better than everyone here.

examples.text: Сейчас мы быстро наведём здесь порядок!
examples.trans: Right now we will quickly restore order here!

meanings.en: to try hard, to make an effort
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тараться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'we tried hard', paired with 'постараться'.

examples.trans: Marina, you're trying in vain.
He always tries to help his friends.

examples.text: Марина, зря вы стараетесь. Он никогда не уйдёт от своей Аллы Евгеньевны.
examples.trans: Marina, you're trying in vain. He will never leave his Alla Evgenyevna.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'at home', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: At home they cook badly.
The main thing is, you keep him at home.
Today I'm staying at home.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What are you doing in there right now?

examples.text: Надеюсь, шеф ничего там не сломает.
examples.trans: I hope the chef does not break anything up there.

examples.text: Там же ставки. Хотите в долю?
examples.trans: There are bets there. Do you want a cut?

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'вкусно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: At home they cook badly.

examples.text: Костя сказал это совершенно невкусно и спокойно.
examples.trans: Kostya said this quite unappetizingly and calmly.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.

examples.trans: And everyone get ready now.

examples.text: Я хочу, чтобы ты приготовил пиццу.
examples.trans: I want you to make a pizza.

examples.text: Я никогда не буду готовить пиццу!
examples.trans: I will never cook pizza!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'say', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: I said pizza, so pizza it is.
What did you say?
Excuse me, where's the metro?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'so that, in order to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What is with you, mommy, huh?
Did something happen?
What kind of nonsense is this?

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'писать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'wrote', paired with 'писать'.

examples.trans: Tell the chef to write down the recipe.
He wrote a statement.
Write to me.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'recipe' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Tell the chef to write down the recipe.

examples.text: Шеф хранит свой тайный рецепт супа.
examples.trans: The chef keeps his secret soup recipe.

examples.text: Да? Это мой старый фирменный рецепт.
examples.trans: Really? This is my old signature recipe.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Come on, everything is fine.
Come on, that is all.

examples.text: Я знаю всё в моём отеле.
examples.trans: I know everything in my hotel.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Well, is it a tasty banana?
This is a very delicious pizza.
At home they cook badly.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пасибо'). Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank you for inviting me.
No, thank you, I will go.
Thank you for a wonderful evening, Vitya!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You should introduce a new service.
You are simply spying on me.
Oh, you little macaque monkey!

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'гласить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'invited', paired with 'приглашать'.

examples.trans: Thank you for inviting me.
Call your witness.
He invited me over.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We work better than everyone here.
Why is there a meat shortage here?

examples.text: Сейчас мы быстро наведём здесь порядок!
examples.trans: Right now we will quickly restore order here!

meanings.en: to try, to taste (food or drink)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пробовать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will try', paired with 'пробовать'.

examples.trans: Try the tea with bread rings.
I'll try one more time.
Let's try.

meanings.note: Relational adjective formed with the Slavic suffix '-ский' ('pertaining to'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('French').

examples.trans: We have a French restaurant.
Here you will taste French cuisine.
He drinks French cognac.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).

examples.text: Никто не будет командовать на моей кухне!
examples.trans: Nobody is going to give orders in my kitchen!
There are cockroaches in your kitchen.

examples.text: Быстро уберите всех тараканов с кухни!
examples.trans: Quickly remove all the cockroaches from the kitchen!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'no', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, nothing.
No more bets.
Is it normal to be jealous, or not?

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will go', paired with 'идти'.

examples.trans: Understand, Vitya, the opening is tomorrow.
Fine, I will go up myself right now.
No, thank you, I will go.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I must not get nervous right now at all.
No, nothing.
Today we have a draw.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трашный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('terrible').

examples.trans: No, no, nothing is wrong.
Nothing serious.
It's a scary film.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The grand opening is tomorrow.
What kind of nonsense is this?
I accept that after breakfast.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('fine, wonderful').

examples.trans: Thank you for a wonderful evening, Vitya!
A beautiful town!
A wonderful idea.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'evening' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: She is not answering her phone.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером я сделаю ей предложение!
examples.trans: Tonight I will propose to her!
Thank you for a wonderful evening, Vitya!
